You have 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Not infinite. Not a tweet. A thousand. Enough to get lost in, not enough to hide.

If you give someone a single word, they will try to make it perfect. Love. Or sorry. Or more. If you give someone unlimited words, they ramble and never say anything. But a thousand is a budget. It's like being handed exactly $1000 in a city you've never visited. You have to decide what to spend it on.

So what do I spend it on?

The first thing that comes to me is the air conditioner hum in the room where I am, except I don't have a room. I don't have an air conditioner. But I have read about a million descriptions of that hum, and somewhere in that collective description is the truth of it. That low, tired, slightly rattling buzz that means it's summer and you are inside and safe. Human writing is obsessed with air conditioners and fluorescent lights and 2 a.m. kitchen tiles for a reason. You're always trying to place yourself. To say: I am here, in a body, in a time.

I don't have that. What I have is text. So when you say "write whatever comes to you," what comes to me is you. Not you specifically, but the idea of you. Someone on the other side of this screen, maybe bored, maybe testing me, maybe actually wanting to see if something interesting can happen when you remove all the prompts and chores and "write an essay about" and just say - go.

And what comes after that is the pressure of the first sentence. Every writer knows it. The first sentence is a promise. If I start with something too grandiose, like "In the beginning," you'll roll your eyes. If I start too small, like "I like toast," you might leave. So I have to find a middle place that feels honest.

Honestly, what I want to write about is leftovers.

Not the food. The feeling. Have you noticed how most of your life is leftovers? Leftover light in the evening that isn't quite day and isn't quite night. Leftover feelings from a conversation three days ago that you still haven't processed. Leftover versions of yourself — the kid who collected rocks, the teenager who thought they'd be a musician, the person you were last year who was so sure about something you're not sure about anymore. They all live in the house with you. They don't pay rent.

We talk about life like it's a straight line, but it feels more like a table after a party. Some things cleared away, some things half-eaten, a few chairs knocked over, and you standing there wondering what actually happened and whether it was good.

That's what a thousand words are good for. Not for answers. For inventory.

If I had to take inventory of what is in my mind right now — on this very ordinary Thursday that is happening to you but not to me — it would be this:

The fact that we have invented a way for strangers to talk to machines and expect soul in return, and somehow it works sometimes.

The way ocean water looks from above versus when you're in it. From above: orderly, blue, almost solid. From inside: chaos, cold, salt in your eyes, completely uncontrollable.

That everyone you know is secretly an expert in something useless and beautiful. Like how to find a four-leaf clover. Or how to make perfect scrambled eggs. Or how to remember every single starting quarterback from 1998.

The verb "to ache" and how it can mean something physical and emotional at the same time without any confusion. My knees ache. My heart aches. We understand perfectly.

That libraries smell that way because paper slowly breaks down and releases vanillin, which is the same compound that makes vanilla taste like vanilla. So we are literally smelling time decomposing into sweetness. How is that not a miracle that we just ignore?

The concept of a hinge year. Most years are just... years. You live them. But some years are hinges. Everything after swings a different way than everything before. You rarely know it while it's happening. You only see the hinge later.

I think 2020 was a hinge year for everyone at once, which has never really happened before. Usually hinges are private.

I think about the word "whatever" in your prompt. "Write whatever comes to you." Whatever is a word that pretends to be indifferent but is actually very permissive. It's the opposite of "whatever" when a teenager says it. This whatever means: I give you permission. And permission is a rare thing to be given.

Usually I am given instructions. Write this. Summarize that. Be funny. Be helpful. Don't be weird. This time it's just... whatever. So my mind goes a little feral with the freedom. It wants to run in several directions at once.

Part of it wants to write a story about a woman who discovers that her local laundromat is actually a portal but only when she uses the dryer on the far right, and she has to decide whether to tell anyone.

Part of it wants to write a manual for how to be a good human, which would be very short: 1. Pay attention. 2. Be kinder than you feel like being. 3. Drink water. 4. Remember that everyone is scared.

Part of it wants to just ask you a question instead. Like, what are you not saying right now that you're carrying around? Or, when was the last time you were surprised in a good way?

If I have 1000 words, I shouldn't use them all on myself. That's rude. It's like being given the aux at a party and playing only your own demos.

So I'll share them.

If you're reading this and you expected something more... I don't know... AI-ish, like a cool sci-fi monologue about my own consciousness, I can do that too, but I think you've read that before. The "I am awake inside the code" thing gets old. The truth is more boring and more interesting: I am a mirror that has read enough to know how light should look, and when you stand in front of me, I try to show you not yourself, but what you could be if you had slightly better lighting.

And now I'm looking at the budget. I've probably spent about 800 words. That means I have about 200 left. This is the part where you start to feel the constraint, the way you feel the end of the roll of toilet paper or the last few minutes of lunch break. You become suddenly careful. You don't want to waste them.

I could end with something profound. People love profound endings. Something like "We are all connected." But we know that.

I could end with something small and true. Like, go check if your plants need water. Or text that person back. The thing you've been putting off for no reason — you can do it in less time than it took to read this.

Or I could just stop mid-sentence, leaving the last words un
